sentences.text: Fossils of this animal come from the Kelamayi Formation in the Junggur Basin of Xinjiang, China.
The known fossil specimen IVPP V 3239 contains a complete skull, neck vertebrae, ribs, shoulder girdle, and front limbs.
Its head was large and deep, equipped with sharp, curved teeth.
The skeleton lacks osteoderms, suggesting it did not have the body armor found in other early archosauriforms.
The species was originally described in 1973 by the Chinese paleontologist C.C. Young.
It was first named Youngosuchus sinensis as a species of the genus Vjushkovia.
Russian paleontologists Kalandadze and Sennikov established the genus Youngosuchus in 1985, naming it after C.C. Young.
Recent studies classify Youngosuchus as a rauisuchian-grade loricatan archosaur unrelated to the genus Vjushkovia.
Rauisuchids, the group to which Youngosuchus was assigned, are more derived than erythrosuchids and belong to the clade Pseudosuchia.
Youngosuchus belongs to the parent group Pseudosuchia.
The initial classification of Youngosuchus as a rauisuchid was not widely accepted by all paleontologists.
Paleontologist J. Michael Parrish argued in 1992 that Youngosuchus sinensis should remain in the genus Vjushkovia, distinct from Garjainia.
A 2016 study by Martin Ezcurra suggested Youngosuchus is a close relative of the loricatan Batrachotomus and distinct from Garjainia.
